"'''Ring My Bell'''" is a 1979 [[disco]] song written by [[Frederick Knight (singer)|Frederick Knight]] and performed by [[Anita Ward]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Harrison |first=Ja'Qaylin |title=Revisiting 'Ring My Bell' with Anita Ward |url=https://uwfvoyager.com/1756/features/revisiting-ring-my-bell-with-anita-ward/ |access-date=2025-08-20 |website=The Voyager}}</ref> 

"Ring My Bell" went to number one in June 1979 on the US [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]], the Disco Top 80 chart and the Soul Singles chart.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2018-08-18 |title=Ring My Bell |url=https://musicchartsarchive.com/singles/anita-ward/ring-my-bell |access-date=2025-08-20 |website=Music Charts Archive |language=en}}</ref> It also reached number one on the [[UK singles chart]].<ref name="UK"/><ref>{{cite book|first= David |last= Roberts |year= 2006 |title= British Hit Singles & Albums |edition= 19th |location= London |publisher= Guinness World Records Limited |page= 591 |isbn= 1-904994-10-5}}</ref> The song's popularity led to Ward's nomination for [[Grammy Award for Best Female R&B Vocal Performance|Best Female R&B Vocal Performance]] at the [[22nd Annual Grammy Awards|1980 Grammy Awards]].<ref>{{cite web|title= Anita Ward |website= [[Grammy Award|Grammy.com]] |access-date= May 3, 2018 |url= https://www.grammy.com/artists/anita-ward/7269}}</ref>

The song was originally written for eleven-year-old [[Stacy Lattisaw]] as a [[teenybopper]] song about children talking on the telephone.<ref>{{cite web |title="Ring My Bell" – Anita Ward |url=http://www.superseventies.com/1979_7singles.html |access-date=June 12, 2014 |publisher=Super Seventies}}</ref> When Lattisaw signed with a different label, American singer and musician [[Anita Ward]] was asked to sing it instead, and it became her [[One-hit wonder|only major hit]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Ring My Bell by Anita Ward |url=http://www.songfacts.com/detail.php?id=5548 |access-date=June 12, 2014 |website=Songfacts}}</ref>

"Ring My Bell" is a 1979 disco song written by Frederick Knight and performed by Anita Ward. 

"Ring My Bell" went to number one in June 1979 on the US Billboard Hot 100, the Disco Top 80 chart and the Soul Singles chart. It also reached number one on the UK singles chart. The song's popularity led to Ward's nomination for Best Female R&B Vocal Performance at the 1980 Grammy Awards.

The song was originally written for eleven-year-old Stacy Lattisaw as a teenybopper song about children talking on the telephone. When Lattisaw signed with a different label, American singer and musician Anita Ward was asked to sing it instead, and it became her only major hit.

sections.heading: Composition
sections.wikitext:
The song is noted for its innovative use of the [[Synare]] [[electronic drum]], playing a decaying high-pitched [[Tom drum|tom]] tone on the first beat of every bar. It also uses [[Tubular bells|chimes]]. The lyrics concern a woman encouraging her partner to relax with her after a hard day at work.<ref name="sexiest"/>

The lyric "You can ring my bell" was seen as sexually suggestive according to 1984 book ''The Slanguage of Sex'', "'You can ring my bell any time you want to' would be regarded as a 'come-on' phrase in the US if used by a female," and "Songs like 'Ring My Bell' by Anita Ward caused scarcely a raised eyebrow in the '70s."<ref>{{cite book|first1= Brigid |last1= McConville |first2= John |last2= Shearlaw |year= 1984 |title= The Slanguage of Sex |publisher= Macdonald |page= 31 |isbn= 9780356103402 |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=1U4bAAAAYAAJ}}</ref> Songwriter [[Frederick Knight (singer)|Frederick Knight]], however, said that he deliberately avoided any overly suggestive lyrics, wanting to project a clean-cut image for Ward.<ref>{{cite magazine|first= Paul |last= Grein |title= Memphis Teacher's Disk Cracks Top 10 |magazine= [[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]] |date= June 9, 1979 |page= 9 |issn= 0006-2510 |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=CCQEAAAAMBAJ&q=%22Anita+Ward%22&pg=PT8}}</ref>

The lyric "You can ring my bell" was seen as sexually suggestive according to 1984 book The Slanguage of Sex, "'You can ring my bell any time you want to' would be regarded as a 'come-on' phrase in the US if used by a female," and "Songs like 'Ring My Bell' by Anita Ward caused scarcely a raised eyebrow in the '70s." Songwriter Frederick Knight, however, said that he deliberately avoided any overly suggestive lyrics, wanting to project a clean-cut image for Ward.

sections.heading: Legacy
sections.wikitext:
In October 2000, [[VH1]] ranked "Ring My Bell" No. 53 in its list of 100 Greatest Dance Songs.<ref>{{cite web|title=100 Greatest Dance Songs|url=http://vh-1.com/insidevh1/shows/100greatestlist/100dance.jhtml|publisher=[[VH1]]|date=October 2000|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20020324113157/http://vh-1.com/insidevh1/shows/100greatestlist/100dance.jhtml|archive-date=March 24, 2002|access-date=April 11, 2025}}</ref> In 2010, ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' magazine included it in its list of the 50 Sexiest Songs of All Time.<ref name="sexiest">{{cite magazine|title= The 50 Sexiest Songs Of All Time |magazine= [[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]] |date= February 11, 2010 |access-date= October 13, 2016 |url= http://www.billboard.com/articles/list/959432/the-50-sexiest-songs-of-all-time}}</ref> In 2020, ''[[Slant Magazine]]'' ranked "Ring My Bell" No. 80 in its 100 Best Dance Songs of All Time list.<ref>{{cite magazine|author=Slant Staff|title=The 100 Best Dance Songs of All Time|url=https://www.slantmagazine.com/music/100-greatest-dance-songs/|magazine=[[Slant Magazine]]|date=June 15, 2020|accessdate=April 10, 2025}}</ref> The significance of the song to the history of [[disco]] is discussed in Episode 3 of the 2024 [[PBS]] series ''Disco: Soundtrack of a Revolution''.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.pbs.org/video/stayin-alive-wvvwry/ | title=Disco: Soundtrack of a Revolution | Stayin' Alive | Episode 3 | website=[[PBS]] }}</ref> Same year, ''[[Forbes]]'' ranked it No. 12 in its list of the 30 Greatest Disco Songs of All Time.<ref>{{cite magazine|first=Jacqueline|last=Schneider|title=The 30 Greatest Disco Songs Of All Time|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/entertainment/article/best-disco-songs/|magazine=[[Forbes]]|date=April 27, 2024|accessdate=April 11, 2025}}</ref>

In March 2025, ''Billboard'' ranked it No. 33 in its list of the 100 Best Dance Songs of All Time, writing, "Anita Ward was working as a substitute teacher in [[Memphis, Tennessee|Memphis]] when she recorded "Ring My Bell", a disco song that became her only major hit. 

The track was written by [[Frederick Knight (singer)|Frederick Knight]], who had minor success in the early 1970s with the famed soul outfit [[Stax Records]]. Knight initially penned "Ring My Bell" for the young singer [[Stacy Lattisaw]], envisioning a song about teenagers chatting on the phone. This origin story is often disputed, as the opening lyric was often interpreted as a double entendre: ''You can ring my bell, anytime, anywhere.'' The instrumentation is pleasingly plush, with a whooping sound accenting the first beat, guitars pawing around the edges of the drums, and a chiming motif that pairs perfectly with Ward's flirty hook."<ref>{{cite magazine|first1=Andrea|last1=Domanick|first2=Andrew|last2=Unterberger|first3=Elias|last3=Leight|first4=Eric|last4=Renner Brown|first5=Jason|last5=Lipshutz|first6=Joe|last6=Lynch|first7=Kat|last7=Bein|first8=Katie|last8=Bein|first9=Krystal|last9=Rodriguez|first10=Lily|last10=Moayeri|first11=Melinda|last11=Newman|first12=Thomas|last12=Smith|first13=Zei|last13=McCarthy|url=https://www.billboard.com/lists/best-dance-songs-all-time/|title=The 100 Best Dance Songs of All Time: Staff List|magazine=[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]|date=March 28, 2025|access-date=April 6, 2025}}</ref>

In October 2000, VH1 ranked "Ring My Bell" No. 53 in its list of 100 Greatest Dance Songs. In 2010, Billboard magazine included it in its list of the 50 Sexiest Songs of All Time. In 2020, Slant Magazine ranked "Ring My Bell" No. 80 in its 100 Best Dance Songs of All Time list. The significance of the song to the history of disco is discussed in Episode 3 of the 2024 PBS series Disco: Soundtrack of a Revolution. Same year, Forbes ranked it No. 12 in its list of the 30 Greatest Disco Songs of All Time.

In March 2025, Billboard ranked it No. 33 in its list of the 100 Best Dance Songs of All Time, writing, "Anita Ward was working as a substitute teacher in Memphis when she recorded "Ring My Bell", a disco song that became her only major hit. 

The track was written by Frederick Knight, who had minor success in the early 1970s with the famed soul outfit Stax Records. Knight initially penned "Ring My Bell" for the young singer Stacy Lattisaw, envisioning a song about teenagers chatting on the phone. This origin story is often disputed, as the opening lyric was often interpreted as a double entendre: You can ring my bell, anytime, anywhere. The instrumentation is pleasingly plush, with a whooping sound accenting the first beat, guitars pawing around the edges of the drums, and a chiming motif that pairs perfectly with Ward's flirty hook."

sections.wikitext: In June 2026, English rapper [[Aitch (rapper)|Aitch]] released "RMB (Ring My Bell)", a UK rap and pop dance rework produced in collaboration with [[Bou (musician)|Bou]] that samples Anita Ward's original.<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Taylor |first=Sam |date=2026-06-12 |title=Aitch has put a fresh spin on Anita Ward's 'Ring My Bell' with new single 'RMB' |url=https://readdork.com/news/aitch-rmb-ring-my-bell-new-single |access-date=2026-07-15 |magazine=[[Dork (magazine)|Dork]] |language=en}}</ref> This track went viral on video platform TikTok, being used in football edits during the 2026 FIFA World Cup and became associated with England's victory over Mexico in the Azteca Stadium.
sections.text: In June 2026, English rapper Aitch released "RMB (Ring My Bell)", a UK rap and pop dance rework produced in collaboration with Bou that samples Anita Ward's original. This track went viral on video platform TikTok, being used in football edits during the 2026 FIFA World Cup and became associated with England's victory over Mexico in the Azteca Stadium.
